newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan, India work towards joint statement.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan, India work towards joint statement.

text.p: Pakistani and Indian negotiators said on Sunday they were close to agreement on a joint statement after a session of peace talks held within sight of the mountains of disputed Kashmir.

"We are very close to a final agreement which will emerge in the form of a joint statement. We will be having a closing session tonight," said Pakistani foreign ministry secretary Shamshad Ahmad, flanked by his Indian counterpart Salman Haider.

"We will finalise this document in the closing session tonight. I cannot indicate the time, but it will be some time tonight so that we can face you tomorrow morning with smiling faces," he told reporters, referring to a news conference planned for Monday morning before the Indian negotiators leave.

The two delegations spent about six hours together, including a working lunch, in the stately Governor House in the hill resort of Murree above Islamabad. The negotiators strolled as they talked in the lush gardens of the state guesthouse.

Governor House is located at Kashmir Point, from which the mountains of the divided Himalayan territory, over which India and Pakistan have fought two of their three wars since independence in 1947, are clearly visible.
"We are going for a final session that should be a make-or-mar session," Ahmad said before the third day of talks. Asked later about that remark, he said: "Well, we have made it."
Haider said at the start of the day that the two sides were working on the machinery of future negotiations.
"We have brought all the nuts and bolts with us," he said. "We will examine them and then put them together. We have started tightening the nuts and bolts. Let's hope for the best."
Sunday's talks would aim to produce an agreed document that would contain working papers from both sides and set out the mechanism for future talks between the arch-rivals, he added.
Asked if the two sides had agreed to set up working groups on divisive issues, he said: "Please don't jump the gun."
The current talks follow an ice-breaking round in late March, which paved the way for the two foreign ministers to meet in April and the two prime ministers to get together in May.
The Delhi meeting of foreign secretaries resumed a dialogue which foundered in 1994 over the issue of Kashmir, two-thirds of which is ruled by India and the rest by Pakistan.
